text: If a black hole replaced our Sun right now, Earth would not get sucked in.
As long as it had the same mass as the Sun, its pull out here would be just the same.
So Earth keeps circling, once a year, at about thirty kilometres a second.
But the black hole would be tiny: the Sun's whole mass, squeezed into a ball about six kilometres wide.
And it would be dark. With nothing falling in, there's nothing to glow.
The sunlight already on its way keeps arriving for about eight minutes. Then the sky goes black.
Within a week, Earth's surface would be about minus eighteen degrees, on average.
Within a year, about minus seventy. The oceans freeze over, but stay liquid underneath for ages.
Could you fly over for a look? Get close, and it pulls your feet much harder than your head.
Long before you reached the edge, that difference would stretch you thin. Scientists call it spaghettification.
And the edge itself is the point of no return. Not even light gets back out.
The good news: this can't happen. The Sun is far too small to ever become a black hole.
In about five billion years, it will swell into a red giant, then shrink into a white dwarf.
So the Sun's gravity isn't what keeps you alive. Its light is.
